routes.label: Complete every series to five games

question: Team A and team B play a series. The first team to win three games wins the series. Each team is equally likely to win each game, there are no ties, and the outcomes of the individual games are independent. If team B wins the second game and team A wins the series, what is the probability that team B wins the first game?
solution:
Imagine recording five independent fair game outcomes, continuing with imaginary games if the series has already ended. This preserves the series winner: whichever team first reaches three wins necessarily has at least three of the five recorded wins. Thus A wins the series exactly when A wins at least three of the five games.

Game two is a B win, so A must win three or four of the remaining four positions. There are four ways for A to win exactly three: choose the one remaining position won by B. There is one way for A to win all four. These give five distinct sequences satisfying the given information.

Independence and fairness make all five-game sequences equally likely, so these five admitted sequences are equally likely. If B also wins game one, A must win games three, four, and five. Exactly one of the five sequences has this form. Therefore the requested probability is \(\boxed{\frac15}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Write each actual series as a string of game winners, stopping when a team reaches three wins. We must account for series of different lengths having different probabilities.

Since B wins game two, A cannot finish the series in three games. If A finishes in four games, the only possible history is \(ABAA\). If A finishes in five games, the final game is an A win and the first four games contain two A wins and two B wins. With game two fixed as B, the other B win is in position one, three, or four. The three histories are
\[
BBAAA,\qquad ABBAA,\qquad ABABA.
\]
These disjoint cases exhaust all histories satisfying the given information.

By independence, the four-game history has probability \((\frac12)^4=\frac1{16}\), and each five-game history has probability \((\frac12)^5=\frac1{32}\). Only \(BBAAA\) has B winning game one. Hence the requested conditional probability is
\[
\frac{1/32}{1/16+3/32}=\boxed{\frac15},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
